passage: It had rained all morning, so break was indoors: thirty children in one damp classroom, and Ma'am gone to the staff room for ten minutes. Kalyani's new pencil case, the blue one with the zip shaped like a fish, sat on her desk. Arnab slid it into his bag. When Kalyani came back from the water tap and started searching, he said, 'Relax, I'm just borrowing it.' 'Then give it back.' 'After break. I'm borrowing it, not stealing.' He said 'borrowing' like a magic word. Kalyani's eyes filled. The room was so loud that nobody else noticed. When Ma'am came back, Kalyani told her. Ma'am asked Arnab, 'Did Kalyani say you could borrow it?' Arnab looked at the floor. 'No.' 'Then what's the real word for taking it?' He didn't say it. But he put the pencil case back on her desk.

qa.q: What was special about Kalyani's pencil case?
qa.a: It had a zip shaped like a fish.

qa.q: Why did Arnab keep saying 'borrowing'?
qa.a: The softer word made taking the pencil case feel harmless to Arnab, like something ordinary instead of a wrong choice he had made.

qa.q: Which question from Ma'am helped, and why?
qa.a: 'Did Kalyani say you could borrow it?' showed that borrowing needs permission, and 'what's the real word?' made Arnab face the act without the soft label.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when the pencil case went missing?
qa.a: Kalyani's eyes filled, so she felt upset and helpless, especially since the noisy room meant nobody else noticed at first.

grounding: Shows a child who takes a classmate's pencil case during a noisy indoor break and calls it 'just borrowing' to make it feel harmless.

passage: In the lift of the Dwarka apartment block, Noor made circles round her eyes with her fingers. 'Ooh, look, it's Owl Boy!' The other kids laughed. Eshaan pushed his thick glasses up his nose and stared at the floor numbers. It was the fourth day in a row. When Eshaan's mother met Noor's mother at the gate that evening, Noor said quickly, 'It was only a joke, Aunty. We all joke.' 'Does Eshaan laugh?' Eshaan's mother asked quietly. Noor thought about the lift. Eshaan never laughed. He always got out first and walked fast. 'He... doesn't,' she admitted. Her own mother said, 'Then it isn't a joke, Noor. A joke is when everyone's laughing.' Noor went red. The next morning in the lift, she said nothing about owls. She asked Eshaan where his cycle was parked.

qa.q: What did Noor call Eshaan in the lift?
qa.a: Noor called Eshaan 'Owl Boy'.

qa.q: Why did Noor say 'It was only a joke'?
qa.a: Calling it a joke made the teasing feel harmless and ordinary to Noor, so she didn't have to see it as a choice that hurt someone.

qa.q: Which question turned things around for Noor?
qa.a: 'Does Eshaan laugh?' made Noor remember Eshaan's face and fast walk, which showed the 'joke' was really hurtful.

qa.q: What was the lift ride like for Eshaan?
qa.a: For Eshaan it was a daily dread: four days in a row he stared at the floor numbers, got out first and walked away fast.

grounding: Shows a child who teases a boy about his glasses and calls it 'only a joke', until an adult asks whether he laughs.

passage:
'Dhruv, whose calculator is this?' Manoj Mama held it up from between the sofa cushions.
'Oh. Ankush's. I'm just borrowing it.'
'Does Ankush know?'
'He left it on his desk. I'll give it back. Sometime.'
'When did you take it?'
'Last week.'
'A week of borrowing without asking.' Mama turned it over. 'His name's scratched on the back. He must be looking for it.'
'Everyone borrows stuff, Mama.'
'Sure. With asking. What's the word when you take something without asking and keep it for a week?'
Dhruv picked at a sofa thread. 'I don't want to say it.'
'Why not?'
'Because it sounds bad.'
'That's why the other word is so comfortable, na?' Mama handed back the calculator. 'Tomorrow, first thing, give it back and say sorry. I'll ask you at dinner how it went.'

qa.q: Whose name is scratched on the back of the calculator?
qa.a: Ankush's name is scratched on the back.

qa.q: Why doesn't Dhruv want to say the real word?
qa.a: Dhruv feels uncomfortable and a bit ashamed, knowing the real word 'sounds bad', since saying it would mean seeing the act as a wrong choice rather than harmless borrowing.

qa.q: What did Manoj Mama do that helped Dhruv face it without shaming?
qa.a: Mama asked calm questions about asking and timing, named why the soft word felt comfortable, and gave a clear next step: return it, say sorry, and report at dinner.

qa.q: What might Ankush have been feeling this past week?
qa.a: Ankush was probably worried or upset, searching for a calculator with his name on it and not knowing where it had gone.

grounding: Shows a child who keeps a classmate's calculator for a week and calls it 'just borrowing', until an uncle asks for the real word.

passage:
I'm Bhavna. When I was nine, Kunal in my class had scented erasers shaped like fruits. The strawberry one smelled like real strawberries.

One day at break I took it and put it in my pencil box. When he looked for it, I said, "Oh, I'm just borrowing it."

I didn't give it back that day, or the next. Every time I said "borrowing" in my head, it felt okay, like a normal thing friends do.

Then Kunal started calling me "Strawberry Thief". I told Miss it was mean. Miss asked me, "Bhavna, when did you plan to give it back?"

I didn't have an answer. I'd never planned to.

I gave it back the next morning and said sorry. Kunal said sorry for the name too.

Now I notice when I say "just". Just borrowing. Just joking. It's usually covering something.

qa.q: Which eraser did Bhavna take?
qa.a: The strawberry one.

qa.q: Why did saying "borrowing" make taking the eraser feel okay to Bhavna?
qa.a: The soft word made it sound like a normal friendly thing instead of taking something that belonged to Kunal. It hid the fact that there was no plan to give it back.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Bhavna, and why?
qa.a: When Miss asked when Bhavna planned to give it back, and Bhavna realised there had never been a plan. The question showed what the word "borrowing" had been covering.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt while the eraser was missing?
qa.a: Kunal probably felt annoyed and upset that his favourite eraser was gone, which may be why he started the mean nickname. Hearing "just borrowing" wouldn't have made losing it feel any better.

grounding: A child takes a classmate's eraser and calls it just borrowing, a softer word that makes the act feel harmless until a teacher's question shows it.

passage:
Class 5 teacher's note, Monday

For two weeks Varun has been calling Nitin "Idli-face" because Nitin brings idlis most days. Others have joined in. Today Nitin didn't open his tiffin at all.

When I spoke to Varun, he laughed. "It's just a joke, Miss. Nitin laughs too."

"Did Nitin laugh today?"

He thought. "...No."

"It's just a joke," he said again, more quietly. The word seems to make it feel like something that just happens, not something he chose.

I asked him to look across at Nitin, sitting alone with his closed tiffin. Varun watched for a while and stopped smiling.

Next step: I'll talk with both boys together tomorrow, call Nitin's mother today, and hold a class talk this week about when a joke stops being one.

qa.q: What did Nitin do with his tiffin today?
qa.a: Nitin didn't open his tiffin at all.

qa.q: Why does Varun keep repeating "It's just a joke"?
qa.a: Varun seems uncomfortable once Nitin's silence is pointed out, and repeating "just a joke" helps him feel the teasing was harmless and not really his choice.

qa.q: What turning point did the teacher create, and what should happen next?
qa.a: Asking Varun to look at Nitin sitting alone with his closed tiffin, which made him stop smiling. Next, talking with both boys and Nitin's mother the same day helps make sure it stops.

qa.q: What is lunchtime like for Nitin now?
qa.a: Nitin seems to feel ashamed of his own food, sitting alone without opening his tiffin. The nickname has turned lunch into something to dread.

grounding: A teacher notes a boy who calls cruel teasing just a joke, a softer word that makes it feel harmless and less of his own choice.

passage: In Class 5B at the school in Lajpat Nagar, Naveen's new pencil case was the best in the room: a metal box with a rocket on the lid and a hidden sharpener. On Monday, while Naveen was at the water cooler, Kamal slid it into his own bag. I'm just borrowing it, he told himself. He's got lots of pencils anyway. On Tuesday Naveen searched under every bench, his eyes red. Kamal kept his bag zipped. Borrowing, he thought. I'll give it back. Sometime. On Wednesday, when Ma'am asked the class if anyone had seen a rocket pencil case, Kamal looked at his shoes. It wasn't stealing, he told himself again. He hadn't even used it yet. But the bag felt heavy all the way home.

qa.q: What was on the lid of Naveen's pencil case?
qa.a: There was a rocket on the lid.

qa.q: Why did Kamal keep calling it 'borrowing'?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and guilty, and the softer word let him avoid thinking of himself as someone who steals.

qa.q: What should Kamal do now?
qa.a: He should give the pencil case back to Naveen and tell Ma'am the truth, calling it what it was rather than borrowing.

qa.q: What was the week like for Naveen?
qa.a: Naveen was upset and searched under every bench, his eyes red, not knowing where his special pencil case had gone.

grounding: A child who takes a classmate's pencil case tells himself he is just borrowing it, so the act feels less harmful.

passage:
'Oye, four-eyes, can you even see the ball?' Zainab called across the playground.
A few girls laughed. Payal pushed her glasses up and didn't answer.
Later, at the tap, Payal said quietly, 'Can you stop calling me that?'
'Calling you what? Four-eyes? It's a joke, yaar.'
'You say it every day.'
'Because it's funny. Everyone jokes. You're too sensitive.'
'It's not funny to me.'
'It's just a joke. Relax.'
'You wouldn't say it if Miss Kaur was there.'
Zainab opened her mouth, then shut it. 'That's different.'
'How?'
'It just is. Fine. Whatever.'
Payal walked back to class alone. Miss Kaur, on corridor duty, had heard enough. Before the bell she called Zainab over, and then sat down with Payal.

qa.q: What did Zainab call Payal?
qa.a: Zainab called Payal four-eyes.

qa.q: Why does Zainab keep insisting it's just a joke?
qa.a: She feels defensive and a bit uncomfortable, and calling it a joke makes the teasing seem harmless, so Payal becomes the problem for being 'too sensitive'.

qa.q: What could Zainab do after this conversation?
qa.a: She could stop using the nickname, apologise to Payal, and notice that she wouldn't say it in front of Miss Kaur.

qa.q: How does the daily joke feel to Payal?
qa.a: It hurts; she stops answering, asks quietly for it to stop, and walks back to class alone.

grounding: A child calls daily teasing about a classmate's glasses a joke, making it feel harmless, until a teacher steps in.

passage: Last year I used to take Reena's gel pens from her desk every morning before she came in. I called it borrowing. I'd tell myself, She has so many, she won't mind, and I'll put them back. I usually didn't. Sometimes they stayed in my bag for a week. One day I saw her looking into her empty pencil pouch with her lip pressed tight, and I still told myself it was only borrowing. Then Mummy found six of Reena's pens in my bag and asked, 'Pallavi, did Reena say you could?' The word stopped working. She hadn't. I'd never asked. I gave them all back the next day and said sorry. Reena didn't say anything for a while. Then she lent me the purple one, properly.

qa.q: How many of Reena's pens did Mummy find?
qa.a: Mummy found six of Reena's pens.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi call taking the pens 'borrowing'?
qa.a: Pallavi felt a little guilty, and the softer word made taking them without asking feel harmless.

qa.q: What did Mummy's question do?
qa.a: Asking whether Reena said yes made Pallavi see that taking without asking wasn't borrowing, which led to returning the pens and apologising.

qa.q: How did Reena feel finding her pouch empty?
qa.a: She seemed upset and tense, pressing her lip tight, even though she didn't say anything.

grounding: A child looks back on calling the taking of a classmate's pens 'borrowing', a softer word that hid the harm.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5B, 14 February.

Today Sunita's new pencil case went missing after lunch. It was found in Ritu's bag. When I asked Ritu, she said at once, "I was just borrowing it, ma'am. I was going to give it back." She had not asked Sunita, and she had moved the pencils into her own box.

This is the second time this term. The first time, she called it "keeping it safe".

I noticed how the soft words made it sound small to her. I said, "Borrowing is when someone says yes. This was taking." Ritu went red and cried a little.

We agreed she will return the case and apologise to Sunita tomorrow, and I will call her mother this evening so we can talk about it together, gently.

Disha

qa.q: Where was Sunita's pencil case found?
qa.a: The pencil case was found in Ritu's bag.

qa.q: Why did Ritu call it "just borrowing"?
qa.a: Ritu felt guilty and embarrassed, and the soft word made taking the case feel small and less like her own choice.

qa.q: What did Disha say that helped Ritu see the act clearly?
qa.a: "Borrowing is when someone says yes. This was taking." It replaced the soft word with an honest one.

qa.q: How might Sunita have felt when her pencil case went missing?
qa.a: Sunita probably felt upset and worried about her new case, and confused when it turned up emptied.

grounding: A teacher's note records a girl who calls taking a classmate's pencil case "just borrowing", and the honest word that followed.

passage:
Friday

Today in PT, Tejas tripped over a cone and everyone laughed, and I shouted, "Tejas the Tortoise!" Then I did the tortoise walk all the way back to class. The whole row was laughing. It was just a joke. Everyone jokes.

At lunch Tejas sat alone. I told Meenu, "He can't even take a joke."

But then Mr D'Souza called me after lunch. He said Tejas had told him he didn't want to come to school on PT days because of the "tortoise" thing. For three weeks. I didn't know it was three weeks. They were just jokes. Weren't they?

Mr D'Souza said, "If only one person isn't laughing, it isn't a joke." He's calling Mummy tonight. I have to say sorry to Tejas on Monday.

I don't feel funny now.

Vasudha

qa.q: What did Vasudha shout when Tejas tripped?
qa.a: Vasudha shouted, "Tejas the Tortoise!"

qa.q: Why did Vasudha keep calling the teasing a joke?
qa.a: Vasudha felt it was harmless fun, and the word "joke" hid how much it was hurting Tejas and made it feel less like a choice.

qa.q: What did Mr D'Souza do that same day?
qa.a: He told Vasudha how Tejas felt, said it isn't a joke if one person isn't laughing, called Mummy, and asked for an apology on Monday.

qa.q: How has Tejas felt about PT days?
qa.a: Tejas has felt so hurt and humiliated that he didn't want to come to school on PT days for three weeks.

grounding: A child's diary shows calling cruel teasing "just a joke" until a teacher explains how the target feels, the same day.

passage:
In the village near Sangrur, Gurleen took Hansa's cycle from outside the gurdwara and rode it round the fields for an hour. When she brought it back, Hansa was crying by the gate.

"I was just borrowing it," Gurleen said, surprised. "I brought it back, na?"
"You didn't ask!" Hansa sobbed. "I thought someone stole it. I have to take milk to Nani's."

Gurleen's Dadi had seen everything from the courtyard. She came out and knelt by both girls. "Gurleen, when you borrow, what do you say first?"
Gurleen looked at the ground. "May I."
"Did you say it?"
"...No."
"Then it wasn't borrowing, puttar. It was taking, and bringing back." Dadi's voice was gentle. "Hansa was frightened for an hour."
Gurleen's face crumpled. "Sorry, Hansa. I'll help carry the milk."

qa.q: Where did Gurleen take Hansa's cycle from?
qa.a: Gurleen took it from outside the gurdwara.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen call it "just borrowing"?
qa.a: Gurleen felt it was harmless because she brought it back, and the soft word hid that she hadn't asked and had frightened Hansa.

qa.q: How did Dadi help Gurleen see the act clearly?
qa.a: She asked what you say first when borrowing, named it as taking, and pointed out that Hansa had been frightened for an hour.

qa.q: What was that hour like for Hansa?
qa.a: Hansa was frightened and upset, thinking her cycle had been stolen when she needed it to take milk to Nani's.

grounding: Shows a village girl who calls taking a friend's cycle without asking "just borrowing", until her grandmother names it.

passage: It was snowing in Istanbul. Siddiq, the new boy from Kabul, had a pencil case with tiny planes on it. Selin loved it. On Monday, she took it from his desk. "I'm just borrowing it," she said. On Tuesday, it was in her bag. On Friday, Siddiq whispered, "Can I have it back?" Selin said, "I'm still borrowing it. Don't be so dramatic." At home, her mother saw the pencil case. "Whose is this?" "Siddiq's. I'm borrowing it." "Since when?" "Monday." Her mother sat down. "Selin, borrowing is when someone says yes and you give it back soon. What's this?" Selin was quiet. "Taking," she said very softly. On Monday morning, she put the pencil case back on Siddiq's desk with a biscuit on top.

qa.q: What was on Siddiq's pencil case?
qa.a: It had tiny planes on it.

qa.q: Why did Selin keep calling it "borrowing"?
qa.a: Selin wanted the pencil case and felt a bit guilty, and the softer word made taking it feel less wrong.

qa.q: What did Selin's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She asked when Selin took it and explained what borrowing really means, so Selin could name it as taking herself.

qa.q: How might Siddiq have felt when Selin said "Don't be so dramatic"?
qa.a: Siddiq probably felt hurt and small, as a new boy whose simple request was brushed off.

grounding: In a snowy week a girl keeps a new classmate's pencil case and calls it borrowing, a softer word that makes the act feel less wrong.

passage: During Holi week, Tarun had a lisp, and every morning Ira copied it. The others laughed. When Tarun turned red, Ira said, "It's just a joke! Can't you take a joke?" On Wednesday, Tarun didn't come out for recess. Their class teacher, Mrs D'Souza, found him in the library, alone, and he told her. Before the last bell that same day, she called Ira to the staff room. "Ira, tell me about the joke." "It's nothing, ma'am. Everyone laughs." "Is Tarun laughing?" Ira thought. "No." "When only one person isn't laughing, it isn't a joke to him." "What will you do?" "Say sorry. And stop." "Good. I'll check with Tarun tomorrow." Ira apologised before she went home.

qa.q: Where did Mrs D'Souza find Tarun?
qa.a: She found him in the library, alone.

qa.q: Why did Ira keep calling the teasing "just a joke"?
qa.a: Calling it a joke made the teasing feel harmless and fun, so Ira didn't have to feel guilty or see how hurt Tarun was.

qa.q: What did Mrs D'Souza do well?
qa.a: She acted the same day, asked Ira whether Tarun was laughing, let Ira decide to apologise, and planned to check on Tarun the next day.

qa.q: What was the teasing like for Tarun?
qa.a: Tarun felt humiliated and hurt, turning red and hiding in the library instead of going out for recess.

grounding: A girl calls her daily mocking of a classmate's lisp a joke, and a teacher helps her see the softer word hid how he felt.

passage:
Summer camp, day 2. Noor took two of Pallavi's butterfly hair clips from the bunk. "I'm just borrowing them," she told herself. 
Day 4. Pallavi was searching her bag, eyes red. "My Nani gave me those clips." Noor touched her own hair, then pulled her cap down. Still borrowing, she thought. I'll give them back sometime.
Day 6. The camp leader, Didi, noticed the clips during breakfast. She sat with Noor by the lake. "Those look like Pallavi's. Did she say you could borrow them?" Noor shook her head. "Then what's the real word?" Noor's throat went tight. "Took." "Okay. What now?" Noor went back to the cabin, put the clips on Pallavi's pillow and said, "I took them. I'm sorry. I called it borrowing so I wouldn't feel bad." Pallavi hugged the clips to her chest.

qa.q: Who gave Pallavi the butterfly hair clips?
qa.a: Her Nani gave her those clips.

qa.q: Why did Noor pull her cap down on day 4?
qa.a: Noor felt guilty seeing Pallavi's red eyes, and hid the clips while still telling herself it was only borrowing.

qa.q: What did the camp leader do that helped Noor?
qa.a: Didi asked calmly whether Pallavi had said yes and what the real word was, so Noor named it as taking and returned the clips.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when the clips came back?
qa.a: Pallavi felt relieved and happy, hugging her Nani's clips to her chest.

grounding: Over camp days a girl keeps a friend's hair clips and calls it borrowing, until she names it as taking and returns them.

passage:
Trisha, come, sit by the heater. That winter I was nine, and our Shimla school was so cold we wrote with gloves on. A girl called Kamla had a tin pencil box with a painted peacock on the lid. One afternoon I took it from her desk and kept it in my bag for three days. When my friend asked, I said, "I'm only borrowing it." Borrowing! I never asked her.
Every morning Kamla searched her bag, and her eyes went red.
On the fourth day my mother found it. She didn't shout. She asked, "If Kamla took yours and called it borrowing, what would you call it?" I carried it back to Kamla's desk myself. That is why your Sarita Dadi always uses the plain word.

qa.q: What was painted on the lid of Kamla's pencil box?
qa.a: A peacock.

qa.q: Why did calling it "borrowing" feel all right to young Sarita?
qa.a: The softer word let young Sarita feel less guilty; "borrowing" sounded harmless, so she didn't have to face that she had taken something that wasn't hers.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed things, and why?
qa.a: Her mother's calm question about what Sarita would call it if Kamla did the same; it showed the act without the soft word, and Sarita returned the box herself.

qa.q: What were those three days like for Kamla?
qa.a: Kamla searched her bag every morning and her eyes went red, so for Kamla it was worrying and upsetting, whatever word anyone used.

grounding: An elder recalls calling the taking of a classmate's pencil box "borrowing", a softer word that made the act feel less wrong.
